body:
What is a computer network?

A computer network is a group of connected computers or other digital devices that can exchange information and share resources. A school, office, bank or household may use a network to share files, access a common printer, communicate between devices or obtain an Internet connection.

Devices may be connected through cables or wireless communication. The connection allows information to move between them according to agreed rules called communication protocols. A protocol specifies how devices exchange information so that the receiving device can understand it.

A computer network connects devices for communication and resource sharing. It does not necessarily require access to the Internet.

LAN, MAN and WAN

Computer networks are commonly classified according to their geographical coverage. The 3 important categories for preliminary examinations are LAN, MAN and WAN.

NetworkGeographical coverageTypical example
LAN — Local Area NetworkA limited area such as a room, building, school or office premisesComputers connected within a school laboratory
MAN — Metropolitan Area NetworkA larger area, commonly a town or cityA network connecting several offices across a city
WAN — Wide Area NetworkLarge geographical distances, such as different cities, states or countriesA bank network connecting branches across India

Local Area Network

A LAN usually connects devices within a relatively small geographical area. For example, computers in a school office may use the same local network to access a shared printer or exchange documents. A LAN can be wired or wireless. A wireless LAN commonly uses Wi-Fi.

A LAN is defined by its limited coverage, not by the number of computers alone. A network with many computers inside one building may still be a LAN.

Metropolitan Area Network

A MAN covers a geographical area larger than a typical LAN but smaller than a typical WAN. It commonly connects networks at different locations within a city. For example, separate offices in Surat may be linked through a city-wide communication network.

A MAN need not be owned by a municipal corporation. The word metropolitan describes its approximate geographical reach, not its ownership.

Wide Area Network

A WAN connects devices or smaller networks across substantial geographical distances. A bank may use a WAN to connect its branches in Ahmedabad, Rajkot, Mumbai and Delhi. Large organizations often connect several LANs through a WAN.

The Internet is a global interconnection of networks and is commonly described as the largest example of wide-area networking. However, a private WAN belonging to an organization is not automatically the public Internet.

How a local network reaches the Internet

A school LAN may allow students to share files and printers even when its Internet connection is unavailable. To reach websites outside the school, the network typically connects through a router and an Internet Service Provider (ISP). The router helps direct data between networks, while the ISP supplies connectivity to the wider Internet.

Wi-Fi is a method of wireless local networking. It is not another name for the Internet. A phone may be connected to a Wi-Fi network even when that network has no working Internet connection.

Prelims focus

  • LAN: Local Area Network; limited geographical area.
  • MAN: Metropolitan Area Network; commonly city-wide coverage.
  • WAN: Wide Area Network; connects geographically distant locations.
  • ISP: Internet Service Provider; provides Internet connectivity.
  • A LAN may operate without an Internet connection.
  • Trap: Wi-Fi is a wireless networking method, not the Internet itself.

[IBM, What Is Computer Networking?, sections What is computer networking? and Network types by geographical area, published 2 July 2025, consulted 15 November 2026; Cisco, What Is a LAN?, introductory definition and LAN components, consulted 15 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, Chapter 10, Transport and Communication, pp. 122–123.]

title: Computer Networks and Their Geographical Extent

body:
Understanding the Internet

The Internet is a worldwide system of interconnected computer networks. It allows devices and networks in different locations to exchange information using common communication rules. It is not a single computer, a single website or a service owned by one organization.

The Internet connects many separately operated networks. A message may therefore travel through several networks before reaching its destination. Information is commonly transmitted in smaller units called packets. Networking equipment directs these packets toward their destination, where the receiving system processes the information.

The TCP/IP family of protocols provides fundamental rules for communication across the Internet. TCP stands for Transmission Control Protocol, while IP stands for Internet Protocol. At a basic level, IP supports addressing and delivery of packets across networks, while TCP can provide reliable delivery of data between communicating applications.

What is the World Wide Web?

The World Wide Web (WWW), commonly called the Web, is a system of interconnected web resources that people can access through the Internet. A web page may contain text, pictures and other content, along with links to related pages.

A hyperlink is a selectable reference that can take the user to another page or resource. The ability to move between linked resources is a defining feature of the Web.

The Web uses Internet connectivity, but the 2 terms are not interchangeable. The Internet is the underlying network system; the Web is one of the services that operates over it. Electronic mail, file transfer and other Internet services also use Internet connectivity.

Internet and Web are different

The Internet connects networks and carries data. The World Wide Web provides linked web resources that users ordinarily open through a browser.

Web pages, websites and web servers

A web page is an individual document or resource available on the Web. A website is a collection of related web pages and resources associated with a common identity, usually accessed through a domain name.

A web server is a system that responds to requests for web resources. When a user opens a website, the browser communicates with the appropriate server to obtain the content needed to display the page.

Web pages commonly use HTML, or Hypertext Markup Language, to represent their content and structure. The user does not need to know how to write HTML to browse the Web.

Web browsers and search engines

A web browser is software used to retrieve, display and navigate web resources. Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge and Safari are examples of web browsers. A browser may be used to open a specific web address directly or to visit a search engine.

A search engine is a service that helps users find information and web pages by entering search terms. The search engine searches its index and provides relevant results. It is not the same as the browser used to access it.

TermFunctionKey distinction
BrowserSoftware for opening and viewing web resourcesRuns on the user's device
Search engineService for finding web informationCan be used through a browser
WebsiteCollection of related web resourcesContains or provides access to pages
Web serverResponds to requests for web resourcesSupplies content to clients

For example, entering the address of a known website directly into a browser does not require a search engine. A user visits a search engine when assistance is needed to locate information or discover a website.

The origin of the Web

Tim Berners-Lee developed the idea of the World Wide Web while working at CERN, the European particle physics research organization, in 1989. The early Web system was implemented subsequently, including a browser and server.

This is a historical fact about the World Wide Web, not a claim that Berners-Lee invented the Internet. Computer networking and the Internet developed through earlier work involving many researchers and institutions.

Prelims focus

  • Internet: Global interconnection of computer networks.
  • WWW: World Wide Web; a system of linked web resources.
  • TCP/IP: Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol.
  • A browser opens web resources; a search engine helps locate them.
  • Tim Berners-Lee developed the Web at CERN in 1989.
  • Trap: The Web is part of the Internet, not another name for the entire Internet.

[NCERT, Class 12, Fundamentals of Human Geography, Chapter 8, Transport and Communication, p. 79, section Cyber Space – Internet; CERN, The Birth of the Web, historical account of the 1989 proposal and early Web development, consulted 15 November 2026; MDN Web Docs, Browsing the web, section The difference between web page, website, web server, and search engine, consulted 15 November 2026; IBM, What Is Computer Networking?, introductory discussion of networks and protocols, consulted 15 November 2026.]

title: The Internet, World Wide Web and the Browser

body:
Why Internet communication needs addresses

When information moves across interconnected networks, the network must identify where it is intended to go. An IP address is a numerical address used by the Internet Protocol to identify a network interface and support the delivery of data.

IP stands for Internet Protocol. An IP address is different from a person's name, an e-mail address or a web address. It is used for network communication rather than as a convenient title for a web page.

IPv4 and IPv6

There are 2 important Internet Protocol address versions: IPv4 and IPv6. IPv4 stands for Internet Protocol version 4, while IPv6 stands for Internet Protocol version 6.

FeatureIPv4IPv6
Address length32 bits128 bits
Usual written form4 decimal numbers separated by dotsGroups of hexadecimal characters separated by colons
Illustrative address192.0.2.102001:db8::1

In an IPv4 address, each of the 4 decimal groups represents a value from 0 to 255. IPv6 uses a much larger address space. Both example addresses above belong to ranges reserved for documentation and are used here for illustration, not as the actual addresses of a particular website.

IP addresses do not always remain permanently assigned to one device. Devices may receive changing addresses, and multiple devices in a local network may share a public-facing address through network arrangements. Therefore, an IP address should not be treated as a permanent personal identifier for a particular user.

Domain names make addresses easier to use

People generally find names easier to remember than numerical IP addresses. A domain name provides a readable name associated with Internet resources. For example, example.org is a domain name reserved for documentation examples.

In the hostname www.example.org, the labels form a hierarchy. The ending .org is a top-level domain, while www is a label placed before example.org. A website does not have to begin with www.

The ending .in is the country-code top-level domain associated with India. The suffix is part of the domain name; it does not by itself prove where a website's server is physically located.

DNS connects names with network addresses

DNS stands for Domain Name System. It is a distributed naming system that allows software to find information associated with domain names, including IP addresses.

For a typical website visit, the process works as follows:

  1. The user enters a domain name or a complete web address in a browser.
  2. The device obtains the necessary DNS information, either from previously stored information or through a DNS lookup.
  3. The domain name is resolved to an appropriate IP address.
  4. The browser can then contact the destination server and request the required web resource.

DNS is sometimes compared to a directory because it helps match readable names with network addresses. The comparison is useful, but the system is more flexible than a simple one-name-to-one-number list: a domain may have several associated IP addresses, and different domain names may lead to the same address.

DNS does not search the content of websites. Resolving a domain name is different from using a search engine to find pages about a topic.

Distinguishing 3 related terms

An IP address is used in network communication. A domain name is a readable name that can be associated with network addresses. A URL is a more complete resource address that may contain a domain name together with information such as a communication scheme and a resource path.

Prelims focus

  • IP: Internet Protocol.
  • IPv4: 32-bit address; commonly written in dotted decimal form.
  • IPv6: 128-bit address; commonly written using colon-separated hexadecimal groups.
  • DNS: Domain Name System; resolves domain names using records that may include IP addresses.
  • .in: India's country-code top-level domain.
  • Trap: DNS resolution is not the same as searching for information on the Web.

[ICANN, The Domain Name System, sections IP Addresses, Domain Names, and The DNS, consulted 15 November 2026; IETF, RFC 791, Internet Protocol, address specification; IETF, RFC 8200, Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification, Section 1; IETF, RFC 5737, IPv4 Address Blocks Reserved for Documentation, Section 3; IETF, RFC 3849, IPv6 Address Prefix Reserved for Documentation, Section 2; IANA, .in Top-Level Domain, domain classification, consulted 15 November 2026.]
title: IP Addresses, Domain Names and DNS

body:
What is a URL?

A URL, or Uniform Resource Locator, is an address used to identify the location of a resource and the way it can be accessed. URLs are especially familiar as web addresses entered into a browser.

A domain name is usually only one component of a complete web URL. The URL may also indicate whether the browser should use HTTP or HTTPS and which particular page or resource is requested.

Parts of a web address

Consider this illustrative URL:

https://www.example.org/guide?topic=internet#summary

Its main components are:

  • https: The scheme, indicating the protocol used to access the resource.
  • www.example.org: The hostname that identifies the destination through the domain-name system.
  • /guide: The path identifying a resource at the destination.
  • ?topic=internet: A query component carrying additional information associated with the request.
  • #summary: A fragment identifier referring to a particular part of the resource, when supported.

Not every URL contains all these components. In particular, query and fragment components are optional. The prefix www is also not compulsory for websites.

HTTP: communication between browser and server

HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol. It is an application-level protocol used for transferring web resources between clients and servers.

When a browser opens a web page, it sends a request to the appropriate web server. The server responds with the requested resource or information about the outcome of the request. The browser then uses the received content to display the page.

For example, a browser may request the home page of an educational website. The server provides the relevant content, which the browser displays. This is a common request-response interaction.

HTTPS and secure web communication

HTTPS stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure. It is HTTP communication protected using TLS, or Transport Layer Security.

TLS protects information exchanged between the communicating endpoints by providing encryption and integrity protection, together with authentication of the server identity through the relevant security mechanisms. This helps prevent outsiders on the network from reading or altering the protected communication in transit.

What HTTPS does not guarantee

HTTPS protects the connection to a website. It does not guarantee that the website's information is correct, that the business is genuine or that the site is free from fraud. A deceptive website can also use HTTPS.

FTP and the movement of files

FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol. Its principal purpose is to transfer files between computers over a network.

Two ordinary file-transfer actions are important:

  • Upload: Sending a file from a local device to a remote system.
  • Download: Receiving a file from a remote system onto a local device.

For example, placing a document on a remote server is an upload; obtaining that document onto a computer is a download. These actions are not exclusive to FTP, because web and cloud services can also upload and download files.

Traditional FTP does not, by itself, provide the encryption associated with HTTPS. The presence of a file transfer should therefore not be taken as proof that the transfer is secure.

Distinguishing common Internet protocols

ProtocolFull formMain user-level function
HTTPHypertext Transfer ProtocolTransfer of web resources
HTTPSHypertext Transfer Protocol SecureProtected transfer of web resources
FTPFile Transfer ProtocolTransfer of files between systems
SMTPSimple Mail Transfer ProtocolSending and relaying electronic mail

All 4 protocols may operate over Internet connectivity, but they perform different functions. HTTP and HTTPS are primarily associated with web communication, FTP with file transfer, and SMTP with electronic mail delivery.

Prelims focus

  • URL: Uniform Resource Locator.
  • HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol; used to exchange web resources.
  • HTTPS: HTTP protected by TLS.
  • FTP: File Transfer Protocol; associated with file transfer.
  • Upload sends data to a remote system; download receives data from one.
  • Trap: HTTPS indicates a protected connection, not guaranteed trustworthiness of the website.

[MDN Web Docs, What is a URL?, section Anatomy of a URL, consulted 15 November 2026; MDN Web Docs, How the web works, discussion of HTTP requests and responses, consulted 15 November 2026; MDN Web Docs, HTTPS, Glossary, and Transport Layer Security (TLS), security overview, consulted 15 November 2026; IETF, RFC 959, File Transfer Protocol, Section 1, Introduction; IETF, RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, Section 1.1, Transport of Electronic Mail.]
title: URLs, HTTP, HTTPS and File Transfer
